newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish casinos face threat of closure.
newsitem.headline: Turkish casinos face threat of closure.

text.p: Turkey's casinos face new restrictions or complete closure because of opposition from the tourism ministry.

"It is clear that while the contribution of gaming operations to our economy is way below expectations, the created social damage is gradually increasing," tourism minister Bahattin Yucel said in a statement on Wednesday.
His ministry has prepared proposals to exclude Turks from gaming establishments or outlaw the sector entirely.
"We are ready to present our work to the cabinet of ministers. If it meets tomorrow they may consider it then," tourism ministry spokesman Fabri Canbeyli told Reuters.
"If the cabinet approves one of the alternatives then a draft law will be prepared," he said.
Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said on Tuesday she was seeking to close the country's 76 casinos, increasing pressure on a sector already facing government restrictions.

The Islamist-led government initially imposed restrictions on opening hours and dress after coming to power in late June, but it has had limited success in imposing a previous order to exclude Turks from casinos.
That order, from the interior ministry to regional governors, did not have the force of law behind it.

Earlier this month the tourism minister said the government was pushing ahead with plans to limit casinos to three designated areas. An island near Istanbul and various tourist resorts are among recommended locations.
Gaming industry officials have protested strongly against the government's plans. They say gambling would continue in illegal casinos, or abroad, with no tax benefits to the country.
Yucel said in his statement that government revenues from casinos totalled only $74.7 million in 1995, and $81.6 million in 1996 up to mid-November.
"Then you read in the newspapers about the social consequences: suicides and people losing their houses because of unpaid debts," Canbeyli said.
The ministry's view that casinos make only a limited contribution to the tourism sector was supported by figures which show that 70 to 75 percent of gamblers were Turkish nationals, he said.
However, the ministry would continue work on plans to establish three casino centres until any new ruling from the cabinet or parliament.

He said the ministry was also concerned about the emergence of a monopoly in the casino industry since it began in 1973 and about the impression created in some political circles that the ministry was attempting to transfer ownership of casinos in its own interests.

Controversy over Turkey's casinos was fuelled this month by allegations from opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz that policemen were involved in the killing of Turkey's "casino king" Omer Lutfu Topal in July.
Earlier this month the interior minister Meral Aksener suspended Istanbul police chief Kemal Yazicioglu and five other security force members to assist the investigation of the killing.
Foreign minister Ciller said on Tuesday that casinos harmed family life and that if a new law was necessary to bring about closure then the matter would go to the cabinet of ministers.
